3. Data Exploration

Sangwoo Mo · POSTECH
Industrial & Management Engineering

Where We ArePart I (Lec 2–5): collection, exploration, and preprocessing

Outline: Data Exploration

Three Ways to Read One TableNumbers, pictures, relations: what each of today’s three parts produces

Descriptive Analysis

Central Tendency

Recap: Mean, Median, ModeThree answers to “the typical value”

meanx̄ = (1/n) ∑i xi|median(x(n/2) + x(n/2+1)) / 2|modeargmaxx count(x)
From 9, 3, 1, 8, 3, 6: mean 5, median 4.5, mode 3

Skew and the Three CentersMode at the peak, median in the middle, mean pulled into the tail

nonparametric skew = (x̄ − median) / spositive when the long tail runs right
Only the mean follows the tail, so mean minus median tells you which way the data leans

Trimmed MeanDrop a fixed share from each end and an outlier stops pulling the mean

x̄α = (1 / (n − 2k)) ∑i=k+1n−k x(i),  k = ⌊αn⌋α = 0 is the mean, α → ½ is the median
Cut the ends and a far-out row stops counting, while every row in the middle still does

Robust StatisticsEvery summary comes in a version built to ignore the far end

The split is not about the mean: every summary number has both versions

Variability

Recap: Standard DeviationThe 68–95–99.7 rule

s = √( (1/(n−1)) ∑i (xi − x̄)2 )the square is what lets one far-out row dominate
These percentages hold for a normal distribution and only then

Interquartile Range (IQR)Q3 − Q1, the width of the middle half: it does not care how far the outlier sits

IQR = Q₃ − Q₁Q₁, Q₃ are the 25th and 75th percentiles
Every cut holds the same number of rows, so how far the last one sits changes nothing

Control Limits and the Normal CurveA normal curve puts about 0.27% of its mass outside μ ± 3σ

0.27% assumes a normal distribution with known parameters; estimated limits can behave differently

Case study: Heavy Tails in Price ChangesMandelbrot, 1963: the risk models of the day assumed Gaussian moves

Quieter than Gaussian on most days, and far wilder on the rare ones

Frequency Distribution

Box PlotThe 1.5×IQR whisker rule flags 0.7% of perfectly normal data as outliers

IQR = Q3 − Q1|fences at Q1 − 1.5·IQR and Q3 + 1.5·IQR
The orange dots are ordinary draws from the curve above, and the fences flag every one of them

Histogram as Empirical DistributionTo see the whole shape, stop summarizing and count: the empirical distribution

Split the range into bins and count. No summary number is used at all

Demo: Histogram Bin CountSame 420 numbers, bin count is the only thing changing

1. Compare 4, 24 and 70 bins.   2. Which pattern survives your choices?
24

Answer: Histogram ChoicesRead what changed before choosing a setting

SettingInterpretation
Few binsDistinct peaks can merge
Many binsSparse bars can mimic structure
Several settingsReport stable distribution features
The setting changes the picture; the underlying data stay fixed

Kernel Density Estimation (KDE)Smoothing the histogram trades bin count for bandwidth

f̂(x) = (1/nh) ∑i K( (x − xi) / h )K is the kernel, h the bandwidth
A small kernel on every point, summed. The choice moves from bin count to bandwidth

Visual Exploration

Recap: Five Standard ChartsThe five you already know

Every one of these needs you to already know which columns matter

Data Manifold

Data ManifoldData does not fill the space evenly: it sits on a thinner structure inside it

Most of the space is empty: the points sit on a much thinner structure inside it

Clustering with k-meansIt always returns groups: the same points after asking k-means for three

Ask for three and you get three, structure or not. k is the bin width of clustering

Demo: k-means ClusteringSame 150 points every time, k is the only input k-means gets

1. Compare k = 2, 3 and 6.   2. Can the smallest WCSS select k?
3

Answer: Cluster CountRead what changed before choosing a setting

SettingInterpretation
k = 2Groups merge
k = 3Three groups in this synthetic example
k = 6Groups split; WCSS can still fall
The setting changes the picture; the underlying data stay fixed

Case study: Marketing SegmentationA cluster needs a name to be useful: from a cluster number to a readable persona

A cluster number is useless until someone can say what makes that group different

Dimensionality Reduction

Principal Component Analysis (PCA)Rotate the axes so the spread lands on the first few

The three arrows are the new axes. The longest one points along the widest spread

Choosing the Number of ComponentsKeep components until the curve flattens: the r-th eigenvalue is the variance the r-th component keeps

Four of ten carry 91% here. The 90% line is a convention, not a criterion

t-SNE vs PCAt-distributed stochastic neighbor embedding separates what PCA leaves overlapping

The same digits, twice: the classes overlap on the left and separate on the right

Demo: t-SNE PerplexitySame two datasets every time, only the perplexity moves

1. Compare perplexity 2 and 30.   2. Can a visible island prove a real cluster?
30

Answer: Reading t-SNERead what changed before choosing a setting

SettingInterpretation
Small perplexityLocal islands appear, even in random data
Larger perplexitySome islands disappear
Original dataCheck neighbors, stability and domain meaning
The setting changes the picture; the underlying data stay fixed

Reading a t-SNE PlotCheck stability; axes, blob areas, and gaps do not directly measure the original geometry

  • The axes carry no meaning. PCA rotates, so its axes can be read; these two cannot
  • Blob area does not directly measure density. Dense regions are inflated and sparse ones are shrunk
  • The distance between two clusters is not their dissimilarity. Local neighborhoods are an approximate optimization target

Deep Representation LearningA network can learn the axes for you: the embedding is learned, not designed

Faces placed near each other really are similar, and nobody designed the axes

Time Series

Time Series and StationarityOrder, trend, and seasonality contain information that one mean cannot capture

A changing mean violates weak stationarity; a single average hides the trend

Four Components of a SeriesTrend, cyclic, seasonal, random

Seasonal repeats on a fixed period. Cyclic does not. That is the whole difference

Time Domain vs Frequency DomainThe same signal: a tangled wave in time becomes two bars in frequency

X(f) = ∫ x(t) e−2πift dtthe Fourier transform; the fast Fourier transform (FFT) computes it quickly
What looks tangled in time becomes two bars in frequency

Statistical Exploration

Two Variables

Scatter PlotBefore any number, plot every row: the only two-variable picture that still shows them all

Direction, shape, spread, and the rows that sit apart, all before anything is computed

Demo: Anscombe’s QuartetSame mean, same variance, same correlation, same fitted line

1. Do equal summaries imply equal shapes?   2. Which plot makes the fitted line misleading?

Answer: Anscombe’s QuartetThe same summary statistics describe different relationships

What stays the sameWhat the plots reveal
Mean and spreadDifferent geometry
Correlation ≈ 0.82Curve, outlier and leverage
Line y ≈ 3 + 0.50xA line is not equally informative in every plot
Plot the observations before interpreting a fitted relationship

Fitting a LineA line summarizes the pair; how tightly the points hug it is what r will measure

Most rows sit close to the line. The far one became an exception only when the line appeared

Covariance of Two ColumnsTwo columns can spread out together, measured in the units of both

cov(x, y) = (1/(n−1)) ∑i (xi − x̄)(yi − ȳ)the SD formula with the second factor taken from another column
Blue points push the sum up and orange points pull it down: positive covariance means blue outweighs orange

Pearson Correlationr measures a straight line, not any relation: a scatter plot reduced to one number

r = ∑i(xi−x̄)(yi−ȳ) ⁄ √( ∑i(xi−x̄)² ∑i(yi−ȳ)² )the same thing as cov(x, y) / σxσy
Panel 4 still has a line drawn through it. r near zero means no straight line, not no relation

Spearman’s Rank CorrelationRanks catch the curve that Pearson underrates: does it keep going one way?

ρ = 1 − 6∑i di2 ⁄ ( n(n² − 1) )di = the gap between row i’s two ranks
Replace each axis with its ranking, then run Pearson. The monotone curve reads 0.76 as Pearson, 0.92 as Spearman

Many Variables

Correlation MatrixEvery pair at once: six process variables, but only two groups of information

Speed, vibration and temperature carry almost the same information

Matrix PlotReorder both axes by species and similar samples form blocks along the diagonal

Reordering both axes reveals similarity blocks that a random order hides

Correlation to Cause

What wrote this table?Exploration reads the rows; what the rows mean is decided one level up

The correlation is observed in the table; its meaning depends on the process above it

Causal GraphsThe same correlation can reflect either causal direction or a shared cause

Three structures give one correlation; the correlation alone cannot tell them apart

Takeaway: Look before you summarizeExploration reveals patterns whose meaning depends on measurement and modeling choices
